questions.stem: A bodybuilder training in a 34 °C gym reaches 39 °C, which falls when he rests. Later, with COVID-19, he is again 39 °C. How do the two episodes compare?

options.B: Exercise: raised set point; infection: unchanged set point
options.C: Exercise: unchanged set point; infection: raised set point
options.D: Both: unchanged set point with failed heat loss
options.E: Exercise: lowered set point; infection: raised set point

questions.explanation: Exercise in heat is hyperthermia: heat gain exceeds loss with the set point unchanged. Infection is fever: pyrogens → PGE₂ → raised set point. A, B: Exercise doesn't change the set point. D: Fever does raise the set point. E: The set point isn't lowered in exercise.

questions.stem: A resting person in a room at 22 °C loses most body heat by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Radiation accounts for about 60% of heat loss at rest. A, C: Conduction and convection are smaller at rest. B: Evaporation (sweating) becomes important in heat and exercise, not at rest in a cool room. D: Respiratory loss is minor.

questions.stem: A tumor destroys the anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area). Which response is most impaired?

options.E: Brown fat thermogenesis in the cold

questions.explanation: Warm-sensitive neurons of the anterior hypothalamus/POA drive heat dissipation: sweating and skin vasodilation. A, C: Shivering and vasoconstriction come from cold-sensitive neurons in the posterior hypothalamus. D, E: These are heat-production and conservation responses, not anterior-hypothalamus heat loss.

questions.stem: At the onset of fever, a patient shivers under blankets although his temperature is 37.5 °C. Why?
questions.explanation: Pyrogens → PGE₂ raise the set point above body temperature, so the body responds as if cold (chills, shivering). A: Set point below body temperature drives heat loss (as when fever breaks). B: Failed heat dissipation is hyperthermia, with an unchanged set point. C: Sweating is a heat-loss response, not the cause of chills. E: Thyroid hormone isn't the trigger.

questions.stem: During general anesthesia with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a 20-year-old develops rigidity, hypercapnia, and a temperature of 41 °C. Which best describes his thermoregulatory state?

options.A: Fever: pyrogens raise the set point

questions.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is a cause of hyperthermia listed in the lecture: uncontrolled muscle heat production with no change in set point. A: No pyrogens or PGE₂ are involved, so antipyretics don't help. C: Temperature is high. D: In hyperthermia the set point is unchanged. E: Circadian swing is only ~0.6 °C.

questions.stem: A newborn exposed to cold maintains temperature without shivering. Which mechanism is mainly responsible?
questions.explanation: Non-shivering thermogenesis in brown fat is most important in infants exposed to cold. B: Thyroid hormone mediates long-term cold adaptation, not the newborn's immediate response. C: Vasodilation loses heat. D: Progesterone raises basal temperature in the luteal phase. E: Sweating promotes heat loss.

questions.stem: Sweating during heat stress is reduced by a drug that blocks the transmitter at the sweat gland. Which fibers normally drive this sweating?
questions.explanation: The anterior hypothalamus/POA sends impulses through the spinal cord and sympathetic cholinergic fibers to the sweat glands. A: Circulating epinephrine/norepinephrine can stimulate sweat glands (important in exercise), but the nerve fibers are cholinergic. B: Sweat glands receive sympathetic, not parasympathetic, innervation. D: Somatic fibers supply skeletal muscle. E: Not a sweat-gland pathway.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man is found outdoors on a winter morning with a core temperature of 28 °C. What is the most likely cause of death if he is not rewarmed?
questions.explanation: Severe hypothermia (27–29 °C) causes cardiac fibrillation; arrhythmias are the common cause of death, and the elderly are a risk group. B: Heat stroke occurs at 40–44 °C. C, D, E: Not the lecture's cause of death in hypothermia.
